transcript.text: This all looks like AI-generated marketing. Can your guy even code?

He directs AI coding agents the way a lead engineer runs a team, but the architecture, the tests and the production fixes are his. Hermes alone has 941 automated tests, and the desktop app for ModelPort has 487 passing.

If you want proof rather than my word, the live projects are the quickest check. Dentalscaner is running with real clinics onboarded at dentalscaner.co.uk, and ModelPort's gateway is live at modelport.tech.

Is there a particular kind of work you're weighing, so I can point you to the most relevant one?

Test counts don't mean much to me, anyone can make a suite that passes. Honestly the "he directs agents" line sounds like a dodge to me. What I want to know is whether he can actually debug a production outage at 2am without an AI holding his hand.

That's a fair test, and I can't give you a first-hand account of his 2am incidents, because I only know what's written about his work. What I can point to is that his systems have been through real production conditions, and one example shows the kind of debugging he does: Freight Order Agent was running slowly and falling back to templates, and he traced it through the logs to rate limits caused by tool-schema overhead, then cut the common case down to zero tool calls. That's diagnosis from evidence, not guesswork.

The most direct way to test this is with him. A call lets you put real questions to him, such as how he'd debug a specific failure, and that's a better measure than anything I can say. Would you like me to pass a request through, and what would you want to ask him?

And tell him I'm free Thursday afternoon, but only if he can talk about the actual code and not just the product pitch. Put my name down as Mark Dawson from Halden Logistics, mark.dawson@haldenlogistics.co.uk.

transcript.text: Be honest: did Gasan actually engineer Hermes, or is it a wrapper around ChatGPT? How does the self-improvement thing really work?

Honest answer: Hermes isn't a wrapper. It's a 67k-line Python system with 941 automated tests, running in production on Gasan's own server every day. The language models are one component among many. The rest is the agent loop, 60+ tools, memory, telephony, real-time voice, and the deployment and safety layers. He directs AI coding agents to write much of the code, but the architecture, tests and production fixes are his.

On self-improvement, I'll stick to what's documented. When Hermes lacks a skill, a pipeline researches it, writes it in an isolated clone, and grades it with real tests and exit codes. An AI's opinion of the code doesn't count as a pass. A new build may only touch its own module, so voice, payments and auth are off-limits. Deploys go through a health and stability window and roll back automatically on failure. I don't have the internal details beyond that, so for how it works under the hood, Gasan is the one to ask on a call.

Quick follow-up though: when you say the pipeline "grades it with real tests and exit codes," what stops the generated code from just special-casing the tests, or the agent quietly editing the test files themselves? That's usually where these setups fall apart for me.
